18	  session's secret set, which §4.1 keeps off the frame. Putting
19	  `last_message` on `SessionView` would send unmasked text from a frame
20	  answer. So no `SessionView` change: the page fetches
21	  `sessions/{id}/last-response` for each Claude session, as the headset
22	  does (`client/Sources/SwitchboardUI/BrowserView.swift:149-163`), and
23	  only when that session's `last_stop_at_ms` differs from what it holds.

106	### Decision 1: browser trust in the certificate
107	
108	**Picked: the click-through on the local network is the trust step, said
109	in the dialog. The host does not offer the certificate for download in
110	this cut.** Why: a download or profile install is a second trust
111	mechanism with its own surface (a route that serves a certificate before
112	pairing, a profile format, what iOS asks of a manually trusted
113	certificate), and the only evidence that it fixes `wss://` on Safari is
114	two sources of 2021 and 2026 (Settled), against Unresolved 1-3, which no
115	experiment here can settle. It is the follow-up if owner question A
116	comes back unfavourable (named at the end).
117	
118	What the click-through buys, and what it does not (the dialog says this
119	in two sentences, and §5 of the spec is amended to say it):
120	
121	- It lets the owner open the page. It proves nothing about who answered.
122	- The `key` in the URL lets the genuine page refuse to send the code to a
123	  host whose `/info` presents a different `spki_sha256`. That catches the
124	  right page on the wrong genuine host (a second installation on that
125	  address or port, a rotated key). A page served by an impostor is not a
126	  genuine page and checks nothing; a page cannot read the key of the TLS
127	  connection it is on, so even the genuine check proves only that the host
128	  claims that key. §5's sentence "a relayed request through a substituted
129	  certificate fails" stands for native clients and is amended: it does not
130	  hold for a browser.
131	- What bounds the damage: the code is single-use and short-lived
132	  (Settled), the pairing window shows scope, and the owner sees the new
133	  device in the dialog and can revoke it.
134	
135	The reissue (above) gives the certificate `serverAuth`, a validity of 800
136	days (under 825, Unresolved 3: if the rule does not bind a manually
137	trusted leaf, nothing is lost), and SANs for `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`,
138	the outward address from `local_address()` as an IP SAN, and, on macOS,
139	`<LocalHostName>.local` as a DNS SAN (Unresolved 2 and 9: both forms are
140	present, so whichever Safari accepts is there). The dialog says the
141	certificate is renewed (key, and so pin, unchanged) and that a changed
142	address means a new browser warning (Unresolved 7).
143	
144	The page's default is REST polling every 5 seconds plus a refetch of the
145	open session. When `new WebSocket` opens, the page switches to events
146	and stops polling; when it fails or closes, the page says "Live updates
147	unavailable, refreshing every 5 s" and polls. This is the same page
148	whether Unresolved 1 comes back favourable or not; the socket is the
149	enhancement, built behind the polling and not in front of it.
150	`crypto.randomUUID` is used only when `window.isSecureContext`, with a
151	`getRandomValues` fallback otherwise (Unresolved 4).

153	### Decision 2: how the token reaches the host
154	
155	**Picked: an `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict` cookie, set by the
156	`/pair` reply, carried by `fetch` and by the socket handshake. The page's
157	script never sees the token. Nothing in `localStorage`, no subprotocol
158	token.** That is the safer store (a script on the origin can read
159	`localStorage`; it cannot read an HttpOnly cookie), so it is the one this
160	plan builds. The facts file's Owner D says the server accepts all three
161	transports; this plan builds one (plus the bearer header the native
162	clients use) and does not build the other two.
163	
164	Mechanics that are unresolved are the implementer's first test, before
165	any other page code (Unresolved 5): on Safari, Chrome and Firefox with the
166	reissued certificate, does a `Secure` cookie set by `/pair` over an IP
167	host come back on a same-origin `fetch`? (This is the basic behaviour; the
168	`__Host-` prefix needs `Secure`, `Path=/`, no `Domain`, all met.) Does it
169	come back on a same-origin `new WebSocket` handshake? If the `fetch` half
170	fails, the finding goes to the owner as a follow-up and no
171	`localStorage` or subprotocol transport is added in this commit. If only
172	the socket half fails, nothing changes: the page polls (decision 1).

174	Host side:
175	
176	- `read_request` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:444-513`) keeps three more
177	  headers, as the bearer is kept, so none are logged with the rest:
178	  `cookie`, `origin`, `host`. `RemoteRequest` (`:360`) gains
179	  `cookie: Option<String>`, `origin: Option<String>`,
180	  `host: Option<String>`. Settled: only `adapters/remote.rs` builds it,
181	  and no test constructs it.
182	- The token is the bearer if present, else the cookie named
183	  `__Host-sb-<server_id>` (per-installation name: Settled says cookies are
184	  not isolated by port, so two instances on one Mac would otherwise

186	  `RemoteRequest::token(&self, server_id)`; the cookie value is checked

188	- **Origin check.** A cookie is ambient: `SameSite=Strict` is by site, and
189	  a site includes every port on the host, so another page on another port
190	  of this Mac is same-site. For a request authenticated by the cookie (no
191	  bearer), any method but GET and any WebSocket upgrade must carry an
192	  `Origin` equal to `https://` + the request's `Host` header, compared
193	  case-insensitively; otherwise `403 forbidden_origin`, no side effect.

195	  this correct for an IP, a `.local` name or loopback. Bearer-authenticated
196	  requests are exempt: a header is not ambient. This answers the owner
197	  question on `Origin`, and it is a security decision, so it is decided

281	### The page's protocol (`web/app.js`)
282	
283	Order on load: (1) if `location.search` has `code`, hold `code`, `key`,
284	`id` in variables and call `history.replaceState(null, "",
285	location.pathname)` as the first statement; (2) `GET /api/v1/info`;
286	(3) with a code: refuse to continue unless `info.spki_sha256 === key` and
287	`info.server_id === id`, else say "this is not the host whose code was
288	scanned" and send nothing; (4) `POST /api/v1/pair {code, device_name,
289	spki_sha256, transport: "cookie"}`; on success store the marker and
290	continue, on `403 pairing_closed|wrong_code|wrong_key` say which, plainly;
291	(5) with no code and a marker: if `info.server_id` equals the marker's and
292	the key differs, "identity changed, pair again" and send nothing; (6)
293	`GET /api/v1/device` for the name and current scope; a 401 is the revoked
294	or never-paired state above.
295	
296	After that it speaks §4.2 and §4.4: every reply is the envelope
297	`{epoch, revision, body}`; one held revision per resource key (a project's
298	session list, one session, one session's `conversation` or `screen`); a
299	reply is applied only at or past the held revision; a changed `epoch`
300	refetches everything. Subscribe first, then snapshot: open
301	`wss://<host>/api/v1/events`, wait for `hello`, fetch `projects` and each
302	`projects/{id}/sessions` (at most 4 in flight), then apply buffered events
303	by revision. `changed {session}` refetches that session and re-sorts;
304	`changed {sessions, project}` refetches that project; `changed {projects}`
305	refetches the list; `removed` drops it; `resync_required` reconnects and
306	refetches. Opening a session sends `watch {kind: "conversation", id}` for a
307	Claude session or `watch {kind: "screen", id}` otherwise, waits for
308	`watching`, then fetches `last-response` or `screen`; leaving sends
309	`unwatch`. Refetch the open view every 30 s regardless (§4.4, covers
310	eviction). Without the socket, every poll refetches the list and the open
311	view; the held-revision rule is the same.
312	
313	A reply is `POST sessions/{id}/send {op, text}` under `control`, with the
314	op made per command. On a timeout the page asks `GET ops/{op}` and follows
315	§4.5: `done` uses the reply, `interrupted` shows the session's state and
316	never resubmits, `unknown` resubmits with the same op. A session with
317	`trust_question` shows "Waiting at Claude Code's folder trust question;
318	answer it on the Mac" and no box; one with `prompt_refusal` shows the box
319	disabled with that reason. Trust, resume, new session, the draft,
320	dictation, Dispatch tickets and the conversation beyond the last response
321	are not on the page (owner question; the API serves them).
322	
323	### `GET /api/v1/device`
324	
325	Authenticated, any scope. Reply, in the envelope: `{device_id, name,
326	scope, server_id}`, read from the core's current device, so a scope change
327	in the dialog shows on the next call. Handled in `serve_remote`
328	(`src/app.rs:3017`) after `authenticate` and before the allowlist match,
329	beside `events`, with no `wire::Body`. No fixture: Swift does not decode
330	it (the fixtures exist for Swift and Rust to agree, and nothing on the
331	Swift side reads this).

# Plan: a web control surface on the remote port (#230)

Line numbers are as they are in this worktree at 7fe8949. Schema versions
as they stand today: `SCHEMA_VERSION = 16` (`src/core/model.rs:12`),
`VIEWS_SCHEMA_VERSION = 7` (`:612`), `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION = 1`
(`src/ports/remote.rs:17`). Only the last moves, and it is written below
as "the value in `ports/remote.rs` at implementation time, plus one".
"Facts" means the facts file for this issue; a line cited as Settled N or
Unresolved N is in it.

## Where this departs from the issue

- **"The one-line excerpt the card shows" is not on the wire.**
  `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:636-688`) has no excerpt. The record
  has `last_message` (written by `src/bin/switchboard-hook.rs:37`;
  Settled, tree), but `remote-client.md` §4.3 says the excerpt is
  "masked from the turn's full text, then cut", and masking resolves the
  session's secret set, which §4.1 keeps off the frame. Putting
  `last_message` on `SessionView` would send unmasked text from a frame
  answer. So no `SessionView` change: the page fetches
  `sessions/{id}/last-response` for each Claude session, as the headset
  does (`client/Sources/SwitchboardUI/BrowserView.swift:149-163`), and
  only when that session's `last_stop_at_ms` differs from what it holds.
  No `watch` is registered for these, so the 128-key watch set is not
  touched by the list. Codex, shell, command and service rows show kind
  and state without an excerpt.
- **"The device's scope in the header": no endpoint returns it after
  pairing** (`remote_info`, `src/app.rs:3568`, is unauthenticated; the
  `/pair` reply is the only place, and it goes stale when the owner
  changes the scope in the dialog). The plan adds one authenticated read,
  `GET /api/v1/device`. This is the single new read model; the page
  cannot show a current scope without it.
- **"Revoked said plainly" cannot be told from "never paired" by the
  host's answer.** `authenticate` (`src/app.rs:3127-3153`) refuses both
  with `401 unauthorized`, and with an HttpOnly cookie the page cannot
  see whether it holds a token. The page keeps a non-secret marker
  (`server_id`, `device_id`, key hash, name) in `localStorage`. A 401
  with a marker says "This browser is no longer paired (it was revoked on
  the host, or the browser dropped its cookie). Pair again." A 401 with
  no marker says how to pair. "Identity changed, pair again" is the
  marker's `server_id` matching `/info` with a different key hash.
  No new refusal code.
- **"Any path outside `/api/v1/` is refused" is true but late:**
  `serve_remote` refuses it at `src/app.rs:3023`, after the request has
  taken a slot in the 64-deep channel and a frame pass. With a page, a
  browser sends strays (`/favicon.ico`, a prefetch). The connection
  thread now owns this decision: the three page paths are served there, any
  other path outside `/api/v1/` is answered 404 there, and `serve_remote`
  keeps its own refusal as the backstop.
- **"The browser then trusts that certificate for that address" is not
  safe to build on.** Settled (WebKit 41419, code-server's iPad doc): on
  Safari a click-through can cover the page and `fetch` but not `wss://`.
  The page therefore works on REST polling alone and treats the socket as
  an upgrade (decision 1 below).
- **"`history.replaceState` … the code never stays in the history" is
  stronger than the sources.** MDN (Settled) says `replaceState`
  replaces the current entry; it says nothing of what the browser
  recorded before the script ran (Unresolved 6). The plan makes the
  claim the host can keep: the code is single-use and the window closes
  at the first pairing, three failures or five minutes (Settled,
  `src/core/remote.rs:46-72`), so a recorded URL is dead. The dialog says
  that instead of promising the history is clean.

## The record

No new record kind, no `model.rs` change, no `SCHEMA_VERSION` or
`VIEWS_SCHEMA_VERSION` bump. A browser is one more `PairedDevice`
(`src/ports/remote.rs:96-107`) in `devices.json`, which is a bare
`Vec<PairedDevice>` with no version. Its name is the page's `device_name`
("Safari on iPhone", built by the page from `navigator.userAgent`; the
host already cuts it to 64 characters, `new_device`,
`src/core/remote.rs:166-175`). No `kind` field: the name is enough for
the dialog (decision 6) and the host reads no `User-Agent`. Revoke and
scope change already apply on the next request and revoke closes the
socket.

One record changes: `identity.json`. The certificate is reissued over the
same key (Settled: `KeyPair::from_pem` is already used,
`src/adapters/remote.rs:139,146`; the SPKI is of the key, so the pin
and `spki_sha256` do not move, §5). The reason is Settled (Apple's
rules): the current certificate has no subjectAltName, a CN only, no EKU,
and a `not_after` in the year 4096, so it meets none of the SAN, EKU or
825-day rules Safari applies. Reissuing cannot hurt the click-through
path and may help it (Unresolved 1, 2 and 3 are the open questions about
how much), so it does not wait on them. Two additive fields on `Identity`
(`src/ports/remote.rs:26-42`), both `#[serde(default)]`:

- `certificate_names: Vec<String>`: the DNS and IP names the certificate
  carries, sorted.
- `certificate_expires: Option<SystemTime>`.

Bump `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION` to the value in `ports/remote.rs` at
implementation time, plus one. `identity.json` has no migration step:
`load_identity` is a plain deserialize, so an older file reads with the
defaults (an empty list, `None`), which `bind_remote` treats as "reissue
now". Written through the existing atomic `RemoteFiles::save`.

Rehydration is unchanged: `IdentityLoaded` at launch, devices by token
hash on every request. The pairing window stays non-durable. On the
device, what persists is the HttpOnly cookie (script cannot read it) and
the marker in `localStorage` (not secret: ids and a public key hash).
The cookie is the only place the token lives in the browser (decision 2).

## The signals

### Decision 1: browser trust in the certificate

**Picked: the click-through on the local network is the trust step, said
in the dialog. The host does not offer the certificate for download in
this cut.** Why: a download or profile install is a second trust
mechanism with its own surface (a route that serves a certificate before
pairing, a profile format, what iOS asks of a manually trusted
certificate), and the only evidence that it fixes `wss://` on Safari is
two sources of 2021 and 2026 (Settled), against Unresolved 1-3, which no
experiment here can settle. It is the follow-up if owner question A
comes back unfavourable (named at the end).

What the click-through buys, and what it does not (the dialog says this
in two sentences, and §5 of the spec is amended to say it):

- It lets the owner open the page. It proves nothing about who answered.
- The `key` in the URL lets the genuine page refuse to send the code to a
  host whose `/info` presents a different `spki_sha256`. That catches the
  right page on the wrong genuine host (a second installation on that
  address or port, a rotated key). A page served by an impostor is not a
  genuine page and checks nothing; a page cannot read the key of the TLS
  connection it is on, so even the genuine check proves only that the host
  claims that key. §5's sentence "a relayed request through a substituted
  certificate fails" stands for native clients and is amended: it does not
  hold for a browser.
- What bounds the damage: the code is single-use and short-lived
  (Settled), the pairing window shows scope, and the owner sees the new
  device in the dialog and can revoke it.

The reissue (above) gives the certificate `serverAuth`, a validity of 800
days (under 825, Unresolved 3: if the rule does not bind a manually
trusted leaf, nothing is lost), and SANs for `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`,
the outward address from `local_address()` as an IP SAN, and, on macOS,
`<LocalHostName>.local` as a DNS SAN (Unresolved 2 and 9: both forms are
present, so whichever Safari accepts is there). The dialog says the
certificate is renewed (key, and so pin, unchanged) and that a changed
address means a new browser warning (Unresolved 7).

The page's default is REST polling every 5 seconds plus a refetch of the
open session. When `new WebSocket` opens, the page switches to events
and stops polling; when it fails or closes, the page says "Live updates
unavailable, refreshing every 5 s" and polls. This is the same page
whether Unresolved 1 comes back favourable or not; the socket is the
enhancement, built behind the polling and not in front of it.
`crypto.randomUUID` is used only when `window.isSecureContext`, with a
`getRandomValues` fallback otherwise (Unresolved 4).

### Decision 2: how the token reaches the host

**Picked: an `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict` cookie, set by the
`/pair` reply, carried by `fetch` and by the socket handshake. The page's
script never sees the token. Nothing in `localStorage`, no subprotocol
token.** That is the safer store (a script on the origin can read
`localStorage`; it cannot read an HttpOnly cookie), so it is the one this
plan builds. The facts file's Owner D says the server accepts all three
transports; this plan builds one (plus the bearer header the native
clients use) and does not build the other two.

Mechanics that are unresolved are the implementer's first test, before
any other page code (Unresolved 5): on Safari, Chrome and Firefox with the
reissued certificate, does a `Secure` cookie set by `/pair` over an IP
host come back on a same-origin `fetch`? (This is the basic behaviour; the
`__Host-` prefix needs `Secure`, `Path=/`, no `Domain`, all met.) Does it
come back on a same-origin `new WebSocket` handshake? If the `fetch` half
fails, the finding goes to the owner as a follow-up and no
`localStorage` or subprotocol transport is added in this commit. If only
the socket half fails, nothing changes: the page polls (decision 1).

Host side:

- `read_request` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:444-513`) keeps three more
  headers, as the bearer is kept, so none are logged with the rest:
  `cookie`, `origin`, `host`. `RemoteRequest` (`:360`) gains
  `cookie: Option<String>`, `origin: Option<String>`,
  `host: Option<String>`. Settled: only `adapters/remote.rs` builds it,
  and no test constructs it.
- The token is the bearer if present, else the cookie named
  `__Host-sb-<server_id>` (per-installation name: Settled says cookies are
  not isolated by port, so two instances on one Mac would otherwise
  collide). `authenticate` (`src/app.rs:3127`) takes it from a new
  `RemoteRequest::token(&self, server_id)`; the cookie value is checked
  for length and base64url characters before it is hashed.
- **Origin check.** A cookie is ambient: `SameSite=Strict` is by site, and
  a site includes every port on the host, so another page on another port
  of this Mac is same-site. For a request authenticated by the cookie (no
  bearer), any method but GET and any WebSocket upgrade must carry an
  `Origin` equal to `https://` + the request's `Host` header, compared
  case-insensitively; otherwise `403 forbidden_origin`, no side effect.
  Comparing with the `Host` header, not a list of addresses, is what makes
  this correct for an IP, a `.local` name or loopback. Bearer-authenticated
  requests are exempt: a header is not ambient. This answers the owner
  question on `Origin`, and it is a security decision, so it is decided
  here.
- **`/pair`** (`remote_pair`, `src/app.rs:3606`) takes an additive body
  field `"transport": "cookie"`. With it the reply omits `token`, and
  `RemoteReply` carries `Set-Cookie: __Host-sb-<server_id>=<token>;
  Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict; Max-Age=34560000` (400 days,
  the longest browsers keep). Without it the reply is unchanged, so the
  CLI and the headset are untouched. `RemoteReply` (`:389`) gains
  `set_cookie: Option<String>` and `#[derive(Default)]`; Settled says it
  is built literally at about 15 sites in `src/app.rs` and none in `tests/`,
  so each literal gets `..RemoteReply::default()`, a mechanical edit.
- The cookie goes to every HTTPS service on that host, on any port
  (Settled). It is `HttpOnly`, so it cannot be read by script; it can be
  sent to a service the owner runs on the same Mac. The dialog says so, and
  it is named for the owner at the end.

### Decision 3: one QR

**One URL.** The pairing window's QR and "Copy invite" carry
`https://<ip>:<port>/?code=<code>&key=<spki_sha256>&id=<server_id>`,
built by one pure function in `src/core/remote.rs`,
`invite_url(address: SocketAddr, identity, code)`. It formats the address
through `SocketAddr`, so an IPv6 result gets its brackets (the JSON form
did not). Code, key and id are Crockford, hex and a UUID: nothing needs
percent-encoding. The JSON form is no longer emitted. Settled: the
visionOS paste field, `ConnectionManager.swift`, `BrowserView.swift:106,
883` and the CLI all go through `PairingInvite.parse`
(`client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:114`), so only that
changes: it tries `URLComponents` first (`code`, `key`, `id`, and
`addresses = ["host:port"]`) and the existing JSON decode second, so an
invite copied before the update still pairs. `addresses` stays a list
(`ConnectionManager.swift:483`, `main.swift:120`). The `.local` name is not
put in the URL: owner question B decides that, and the IP works whichever
way it comes back.

### Decision 4: the static paths

- **Paths, exactly:** `GET /` (also with a query), `GET /app.js`,
  `GET /app.css`. Content types `text/html; charset=utf-8`,
  `text/javascript; charset=utf-8`, `text/css; charset=utf-8`. The HTML
  carries `<link rel="icon" href="data:,">` so no `/favicon.ico` request is
  made. Any other method on these is `405` with `Allow: GET`; any other
  path outside `/api/v1/` is `404` with the usual JSON error.
- **Headers on all three (and the 404/405):** `Content-Security-Policy:
  default-src 'none'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; connect-src
  'self'; img-src data:; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'none';
  frame-ancestors 'none'`, `Cache-Control: no-store`,
  `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` (the URL with the code must not leave in
  a `Referer`), `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Connection: close`.
  The page has no inline script, no inline style and no `style=` attribute,
  and no external URL. Whether WebKit treats `connect-src 'self'` as
  covering `wss://` on the same host is not in the facts; the first
  manual run on Safari records it, and the polling path is why a "no" does
  not break the page.
- **Who answers:** the connection thread (`connection`,
  `src/adapters/remote.rs:770`), before the request is handed to the
  frame, because the bytes need no core state and §4.1 says the frame does
  core state only. The bytes are `include_str!("../../web/index.html")`,
  `app.js`, `app.css` in `adapters/remote.rs`. No build step, no
  dependency.
- **Pool and rate window.** A page load counts against the 4
  unauthenticated connections like any stranger (§4.1; unchanged), and
  `Connection: close` frees the slot as soon as the file is sent, so the
  three files do not hold three slots for 30 s of idle (Unresolved 8: how
  many parallel connections iOS Safari opens needs a device). Static paths get
  their own `RateWindow` in `Limits` (`:625-640`), 60 per minute per
  listener, `429` past it, so a page-load loop cannot be charged to the
  `/pair` window (6/min) or the `/info` window (60/min). The page's own
  `/info` and `/pair` calls count against theirs as today.
- **Before pairing the listener serves `/info`, `/pair` and the page.**
  §5's "Require pairing before anything but `/info` and `/pair`" is
  amended to add the page. The page's bytes are identical on every
  installation and carry no host data (no id, no key, no name): the
  host-specific values arrive only in the URL the owner scanned and in
  `/info`.
- **Opened with neither code nor marker:** a plain message: "Open
  Remote devices in Switchboard on the Mac, choose Allow pairing, and scan
  the code with this device's camera." No code-entry form in this cut: a
  typed code without the scanned key would skip the one check the page
  can make. A paste field is the natural follow-up.
- **`refuse` and the code.** The page request never reaches the frame, so
  `refuse` (`src/app.rs:3754`, logs method and path only) is not on the
  path; the static arm logs nothing and never logs the query.

### The page's protocol (`web/app.js`)

Order on load: (1) if `location.search` has `code`, hold `code`, `key`,
`id` in variables and call `history.replaceState(null, "",
location.pathname)` as the first statement; (2) `GET /api/v1/info`;
(3) with a code: refuse to continue unless `info.spki_sha256 === key` and
`info.server_id === id`, else say "this is not the host whose code was
scanned" and send nothing; (4) `POST /api/v1/pair {code, device_name,
spki_sha256, transport: "cookie"}`; on success store the marker and
continue, on `403 pairing_closed|wrong_code|wrong_key` say which, plainly;
(5) with no code and a marker: if `info.server_id` equals the marker's and
the key differs, "identity changed, pair again" and send nothing; (6)
`GET /api/v1/device` for the name and current scope; a 401 is the revoked
or never-paired state above.

After that it speaks §4.2 and §4.4: every reply is the envelope
`{epoch, revision, body}`; one held revision per resource key (a project's
session list, one session, one session's `conversation` or `screen`); a
reply is applied only at or past the held revision; a changed `epoch`
refetches everything. Subscribe first, then snapshot: open
`wss://<host>/api/v1/events`, wait for `hello`, fetch `projects` and each
`projects/{id}/sessions` (at most 4 in flight), then apply buffered events
by revision. `changed {session}` refetches that session and re-sorts;
`changed {sessions, project}` refetches that project; `changed {projects}`
refetches the list; `removed` drops it; `resync_required` reconnects and
refetches. Opening a session sends `watch {kind: "conversation", id}` for a
Claude session or `watch {kind: "screen", id}` otherwise, waits for
`watching`, then fetches `last-response` or `screen`; leaving sends
`unwatch`. Refetch the open view every 30 s regardless (§4.4, covers
eviction). Without the socket, every poll refetches the list and the open
view; the held-revision rule is the same.

A reply is `POST sessions/{id}/send {op, text}` under `control`, with the
op made per command. On a timeout the page asks `GET ops/{op}` and follows
§4.5: `done` uses the reply, `interrupted` shows the session's state and
never resubmits, `unknown` resubmits with the same op. A session with
`trust_question` shows "Waiting at Claude Code's folder trust question;
answer it on the Mac" and no box; one with `prompt_refusal` shows the box
disabled with that reason. Trust, resume, new session, the draft,
dictation, Dispatch tickets and the conversation beyond the last response
are not on the page (owner question; the API serves them).

### `GET /api/v1/device`

Authenticated, any scope. Reply, in the envelope: `{device_id, name,
scope, server_id}`, read from the core's current device, so a scope change
in the dialog shows on the next call. Handled in `serve_remote`
(`src/app.rs:3017`) after `authenticate` and before the allowlist match,
beside `events`, with no `wire::Body`. No fixture: Swift does not decode
it (the fixtures exist for Swift and Rust to agree, and nothing on the
Swift side reads this).

## The actions and effects

One new action, `AppAction::CertificateReissued { certificate: String,
names: Vec<String>, expires: SystemTime }`, handled in
`src/core/remote.rs` through the existing `update_identity`
(`:105-117`), which already emits `Effect::SaveIdentity` and does nothing
when read-only. No new effect, no new port method: `RemoteStore` already
saves the identity.

Adapter: `remote::reissue_certificate(identity, key_pem, names, now) ->
Result<(String, SystemTime), String>` beside `make_identity`
(`src/adapters/remote.rs:95`), over `KeyPair::from_pem`, with the SANs,
`serverAuth`, `not_before` a day back, `not_after` 800 days out; and
`remote::local_names()`, the sorted names above (the `.local` name from
`scutil --get LocalHostName`, absent when the command fails or off macOS,
so Linux CI compiles and passes). In `bind_remote` (`src/app.rs:2935`),
before `tls_config` at `:2957`: if `identity.certificate_names` differs
from `local_names()`, or `certificate_expires` is `None` or within 30 days,
call `reissue_certificate` with the Keychain key already fetched there,
dispatch `CertificateReissued`, and build the TLS config from the core's
identity afterwards. `make_identity` also fills the two new fields. An
address that changes while the port is running is not noticed until the
next bind; that is a known gap in the design status, not machinery here.

Serving the page is not an effect: it never leaves the connection thread.
The request-side changes (three headers, `set_cookie`, the Origin check)
are in the adapter and `authenticate`, with no action.

## The UI

**The pairing window** (`src/ui/remote.rs:155-215`). The `json!` payload
and `qr_texture` input become `core::remote::invite_url(...)`; "Copy
invite" copies the URL and its hover says "The QR code's link, to open in
a browser or paste into a client". The caption keeps the key and code and
gains the trust text from decision 1 (two sentences: the browser will warn
about this host's certificate; accepting it is the step that trusts this
network and does not verify the host; the key in the link only stops a
page from sending the code to a different Switchboard; the link works
once and expires in five minutes or three wrong codes). The paired-devices
section (`devices`, `:230`) gains one line under the table: a browser's
token is an HttpOnly cookie sent to any HTTPS service on this Mac's
address. It uses `GAP` and `PAD`; no logic beyond the format call.

**The page** (`web/index.html`, `app.js`, `app.css`), one file each, no
framework. A header with the host's name (from `/info`), the device's
name and scope word (from `/device`), and the live/polling indicator.
Below: a "Waiting on you" group first (every session with `waiting`,
marked, with `waiting_reason`), then one group per project; each row has
the session name, kind, `card` word and the excerpt. A session view with
the last response (Claude) or screen text (anything else), refreshed on
`changed`, and the reply box under `control`, absent for `read`. States,
each one sentence: not paired, pairing closed, wrong host, identity
changed, no longer paired, host unreachable, live updates unavailable,
`read` scope. Text only, `textContent` never `innerHTML`, since session
text is attacker-influenced.

## The tests

CI cannot drive a browser and the tree has no JS runner (the issue rules
out a dependency), so the page's reconcile logic is checked by hand. The
host's side is tested in full.

- **`src/core/tests.rs`:** `invite_url` for an IPv4 and an IPv6 address;
  `CertificateReissued` updates the identity and returns one
  `SaveIdentity`; it is a no-op read-only.
- **`src/adapters/remote.rs` unit tests:** `reissue_certificate` keeps
  `spki_sha256` (`spki_sha256_of_cert` equals the key's) and `tls_config`
  accepts it; `RemoteRequest::token` prefers the bearer, reads only the
  cookie with the right name, rejects an oversized value; the same-origin
  rule (equal, different port, different scheme, missing, case).
- **`tests/remote.rs`** (extend `http`, `:245`, to return the headers; keep
  the old signature as a wrapper so existing callers do not change):
  - the three paths answer unpaired with the exact `Content-Type`, the
    CSP above, `Cache-Control: no-store`, `Referrer-Policy`, `nosniff` and
    `Connection: close`; `/favicon.ico`, `/web/app.js` and `/%2e%2e/` give

302:## 5. Security and pairing
309:- **Pairing verifies the key before the code is sent.** The code alone would let an intermediary terminate the first connection, forward the code to the real host, and take the token. So the pairing window shows a **QR code** carrying `{server_id, spki_sha256, code, addresses}`, and under it the same in text: a short form of the key hash and the code. The client scans or types both; it connects, compares the hash of the key it is actually talking to with the one it was given, and only when they match sends `/pair {code, device_name, spki_sha256}`. A client without a camera (visionOS gives an app none) pairs from the host's Bonjour record instead: it resolves the record, reads `/info` under no trust, shows the key the host presented in the dialog's short form for the owner to compare by eye, and pins that key for the pairing, so the typed code reaches only the host whose key the owner checked; a substituted certificate shows its own key on the device, where the owner sees it differ. The host refuses a pairing whose `spki_sha256` is not its own, so a relayed request through a substituted certificate fails even if the code reached it. Before pairing, `/info` is served to any client and nothing in it is trusted; after pairing, every connection verifies the pin before the token is presented.
311:- **The code**: eight characters from the 32-character Crockford alphabet (no `I`, `L`, `O`, `U`), 40 bits, drawn from the OS random source (`getrandom`), made when the window opens and shown as the QR's `code` and in text. It is single-use: the first successful `/pair` consumes it and closes the window. **Failures count globally**: one counter in the app's state, bumped on the frame for every failed `/pair` from any connection, and the window closes at three. Concurrent attempts cannot each get three, because the frame answers them in arrival order against the one counter.

The search didn't turn up anything about how `__Host-` handles IP-address hosts, so the IP question is unanswered here.

What the results do cover:

- **Requirements:** The 2015 cookie-prefixes draft says a `__Host-` cookie must be set with the Secure attribute, from a URI whose scheme the user agent treats as secure, and sent only to the host that set it. [draft-west-cookie-prefixes](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-west-cookie-prefixes)
- **Later draft wording:** A Rust cookie library's docs quote RFC 6265bis-12 §4.1.3.2 as requiring the Secure attribute, a Path of `/`, and no Domain attribute. [doc.servo.org](https://doc.servo.org/cookie/prefix/struct.Host.html)
- **Domain scope:** A 2017 httpbis draft says a `__Host-` cookie must not carry a Domain attribute, so it goes only to the exact host and not to subdomains. [greenbytes draft-00](https://www.greenbytes.de/tech/webdav/draft-ietf-httpbis-cookie-prefixes-00.xml)

My inference, not stated in these sources: because `__Host-` forbids a Domain attribute, a cookie set from an IP-address host should be host-only, and the Secure and Path=/ rules would still apply. Note that these sources are drafts and library documentation, not the final RFC 6265bis text, so check the current draft or RFC 6265bis on the IETF datatracker before relying on this.

content.content:
120	### 4.1 Implementation
121	
122	- **No Tokio.** The host is std threads and `mpsc`; the core is owned by `SwitchboardApp` and every state change is a dispatch on the frame thread. The remote port follows the `ControlSocket` shape: an accept thread per listener, one thread per connection, each request handed over a channel to the frame, answered by the same `serve` path in `app.rs` (`serve_pending` runs before every frame, hidden ones included), the reply sent back on the connection's channel. A second runtime inside an egui app buys nothing for a handful of connections.
123	- **The frame does core state only.** A metadata request (a view, a command) is answered on the frame as the control port is. A content request (conversation, screen, run output, file) takes two steps: the frame answers with the **handle and the redaction policy** (the transcript path and resume handle, the pane's host id, the run's log path, the file's root and relative path, plus the secret values to mask and the policy fingerprint), and one **content worker thread** does the read, the parse, the mask, the version check and the serialization from a queue of such requests (one at a time, so one large parse is in memory at once; Spike 22 measured 575 MB peak for the largest transcript), then sends one small action back to the frame to record the version it observed (§4.4), and the connection thread writes the reply. The watch poll (§4.4) runs through the same worker. A multi-megabyte transcript, a 768 KiB file or a slow Keychain call therefore costs the worker its time and the asking connection its wait, never a frame. The handle is read under the frame's authority, so a record removed or rebound between the two steps makes the worker's version action a no-op and the reply carries the handle it read from.
124	- **Bounds.** The port is one user's few devices, and the limits say so:
125	  - at most 16 connections in total and 4 unauthenticated ones; a further accept is closed at once. The 4 are a separate pool: an unauthenticated flood fills its own slots and never a paired client's;
126	  - `/pair` is answered at most six times a minute per listener and `/info` sixty; past that the connection thread answers 429 without reaching the frame;
127	  - a TLS handshake and the first request line each within 5 s, a request body within 10 s, a write within 10 s; a connection that misses a deadline is closed;
128	  - one request in flight per connection (HTTP/1.1, no pipelining);
129	  - the frame drains at most 8 remote requests per pass, in arrival order, the rest waiting on the channel; the channel is bounded at 64 and a full channel answers 503 from the connection thread without reaching the frame; a frame-side request is a view or a handle lookup and takes microseconds, so the count is the bound;
130	  - each WebSocket subscriber has an event queue of 256; when it fills, the subscriber is sent `resync_required` and closed, never silently trimmed (§4.4);
131	  - the watch set (§4.4) is capped at 128 keys for the whole port; past the cap the least recently read key is evicted silently, since a read of an evicted key always works and re-enters it.
132	- Preferred crates: a blocking HTTP/1.1 server over `std::net::TcpListener` (hand-rolled or `tiny_http`), `tungstenite` for WebSocket, `rustls` with `rcgen` for the per-installation certificate, and `mdns-sd` (or the system `dns-sd` through a small macOS adapter) for Bonjour. All of it in `src/adapters/remote.rs` behind a `ports::remote` trait with a fake, and all of it must compile on Linux CI (Bonjour may be a `cfg(target_os = "macos")` adapter with a no-op elsewhere). **Spike 22 (§10) decides the exact crates before any of this is built.**
133	- Handlers are thin: HTTP request → auth and scope check → allowlist → `wire::Request` → `serve` → redaction → `wire::Reply` → HTTP response. No session or transcript logic lives in the adapter.
134	- Only the instance holding the store lock listens (as the control port does); a read-only instance refuses to bind.
135	- Bind to loopback by default until remote access is explicitly enabled in Settings. For LAN access, bind the chosen interface and require pairing.
136	- Configurable port in `identity.json` (§3.1), default `43187`, overridable with `SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT` (a dev aid, documented in the README) so two instances can run on one machine; `0` picks a free one, which the tests use.
137	- Advertise `_switchboard._tcp` via Bonjour only while listening on a non-loopback interface. TXT records carry the protocol major version (`v`), the display name (`name`) and the `server_id` (`id`, so a client matches a record to a known server before it connects); never a token, never key material. The instance name is the display name with a short id suffix, so two installations on one machine stay distinct.
138	- If Switchboard closes, the port goes away. A standalone daemon is not in scope.
139	
140	### 4.2 API conventions
141	
142	- Version prefix: `/api/v1`.
143	- JSON request and response bodies. Timestamps as milliseconds since the epoch, matching the wire crate (`last_stop_at_ms`); the client formats them.
144	- The wire crate's views are the response schemas. New views are added to `switchboard-control` additively (it stays std + serde only, and Dispatch keeps compiling).
145	- Standard error shape: `{ "error": { "code": "...", "message": "..." } }`, with `wire::Reply::Failed` mapped onto it.
146	- **Every response** carries the host's `epoch` and `revision` (§4.4) in an envelope: `{ "epoch": "...", "revision": n, "body": ... }`. The revision is the one at which the body's **content version** was observed (§4.4, "Content versions"), not merely the counter at the time of the reply. The client keeps one held revision per resource key (a session's metadata, its conversation, its screen, one run's output, one file are separate keys) and applies a reply only if its revision is at or past the held one, so an older reply arriving after a newer one is dropped and fetching a session's metadata never invalidates a valid conversation page.
147	- **Caps.** The serialized, masked body of any reply is at most 1 MiB, envelope included, enforced on the output bytes. The rule per kind:
148	  - **collections** (`projects`, `spaces`, `sets`, `sessions`, `runs`, a set's pins, `waiting`) are answered **whole, in one reply, never paged and never cut**. They are small: a data directory holds hundreds of records at most, and a project's session list with every string bounded as below is under 100 KiB at that scale. A collection reply is one snapshot of its membership at one revision, which is what makes a cached member's removal safe: a member missing from a whole reply at a revision at or past the one it was learned at is gone. The 1 MiB cap is enforced on the serialized reply as everywhere; a collection that would exceed it is a bug in the bounds, answered `too_large` and logged, not paged around.
149	  - **metadata views**, in a collection and standing alone, are bounded field by field, after masking: `notes` at 4 KiB in a collection and 64 KiB standing alone, `name`, `waiting_reason`, `cwd` and every other free-text string at 4 KiB, each cut marked in a `truncated` list of field names; no field is left unbounded. A client that wants a session's full notes reads the session alone.
150	  - **conversation** pages stop at `limit` turns or at the cap with `next`; a turn larger than 256 KiB is cut and marked (§4.3).
151	  - **last response** and **run output** are cut from the front (older text dropped) and marked `truncated: true`.
152	  - **file content** is sent whole or not at all: the port's file limit is 768 KiB of source bytes, and a larger pinned file answers `too_large` with its size. The source limit is not a guarantee of fit: JSON escaping can double a file of quotation marks and masking can lengthen text, so the limit is enforced once more on the masked, serialized reply, and a file that exceeds it there answers `too_large` too, naming the serialized size. The client says so on the card.
153	  - **screen** is bounded by `lines` (at most 200) and, after masking, by bytes: text over 256 KiB is cut from the top (older lines dropped) and marked `truncated: true`.
154	- A command is **accepted** when `serve` returns; its outcome arrives through events and the session's state. For `session.send` there is no completion signal beyond the next `Stop` hook event on that record (§4.5).
155	- Document payload schemas with examples; generate the Swift `Codable` types from the Rust views (serde shapes) and keep a fixture test on both sides.
156	
157	### 4.3 Endpoints
158	
159	| Method | Endpoint | Wire body | Scope |
160	|---|---|---|---|
161	| GET | `/api/v1/info` | new: `info` | none (identity only, before pairing) |
162	| POST | `/api/v1/pair` | pairing handshake (§5) | none, only inside the pairing window |
163	| GET | `/api/v1/projects` | `projects`; `?scope=all` includes Dispatch's worker records | read |
164	| GET | `/api/v1/spaces` | `spaces` | read |
165	| GET | `/api/v1/spaces/{id}/sets` | `sets` | read |
166	| GET | `/api/v1/sets/{id}` | new: `set` (the `SetView` with pins) | read |
167	| GET | `/api/v1/projects/{id}/sessions` | `sessions`; `?scope=all` as above | read |
168	| GET | `/api/v1/sessions/{id}` | `session` | read |
169	| GET | `/api/v1/waiting` | `waiting`; `?scope=all` as above | read |
170	| GET | `/api/v1/sessions/{id}/screen?lines=n` | `session.screen` | read |
171	| GET | `/api/v1/sessions/{id}/conversation?from=turn\|last&limit=n`, or `?before=turn&limit=n` | new: `session.conversation` | read |
172	| GET | `/api/v1/sessions/{id}/conversation/{n}` | new: `session.turn` (one turn with its activity uncut) | read |
173	| GET | `/api/v1/sessions/{id}/last-response` | new: `session.last_response` | read |
174	| GET | `/api/v1/sessions/{id}/runs` | new: `session.runs` | read |
175	| GET | `/api/v1/sessions/{id}/runs/{n}/output?lines=n` | new: `session.run_output` | read |
176	| GET | `/api/v1/projects/{id}/files/{path}` | new: `file.read` (pinned files only) | read |
177	| POST | `/api/v1/projects/{id}/sessions` | `session.new` (§4.5) | control |
178	| POST | `/api/v1/sessions/{id}/send` | `session.send` | control |
179	| POST | `/api/v1/sessions/{id}/resume` | `session.resume` | control |
180	| POST | `/api/v1/sessions/{id}/trust` | `session.trust` | control |
181	| GET | `/api/v1/sessions/{id}/draft` | `session.draft` | read |
182	| POST | `/api/v1/sessions/{id}/draft` | `session.draft` | control |
183	| POST | `/api/v1/sessions/{id}/dictation` | `session.dictation` | control |
184	| GET | `/api/v1/ops/{op}` | `op.status` | read |
185	| GET | `/api/v1/dispatch/tickets` | new: the core's `TicketListing` (§4.7) | read |
186	| GET | `/api/v1/dispatch/tickets/{id}` | new: `TicketDetail` | read |
187	| POST | `/api/v1/dispatch/tickets/{id}/decide` | new: the Mac's `DispatchDecide` | control |
188	| POST | `/api/v1/dispatch/tickets/{id}/resume` | new: the Mac's `DispatchResume` | control |
189	| POST | `/api/v1/dispatch/tickets/{id}/close` | new: the Mac's `DispatchClose` | control |
190	| GET | `/api/v1/dispatch/tickets/{id}/files/{key}` | new: the Mac's `DispatchReadArtifact`, or the disk for an image | read |
191	| GET | `/api/v1/dispatch/tickets/{id}/events` | new: the Mac's `DispatchReadEvents` | read |
192	| GET | `/api/v1/events` | WebSocket upgrade | read |
193	
194	Everything else on the wire is **refused before translation**, by an allowlist, not a denylist: `env.resolve` returns secret values; the `env.*` writes, `definition.install`, `project.add`, `project.root`, `set.sync`, `workflow.*`, `dispatch.runner`, `session.kill` and `session.remove` change what runs on the host or what it keeps. v1 remote is the table above and nothing more.
195	
196	**Redaction, one policy for every text that leaves the port, applied before any cut.** `session.screen` today masks the values of the project's secret variables and of the session's granted environment sets, and it reads slack lines above the window first so a value wrapped across the window's first line is still found whole. The port generalizes both halves of that: one `redact` function in `app.rs`, and the rule that **masking runs over complete source text, and every cut comes after**, since a value split by a cut no longer matches. Per kind:
197	  - **conversation**: the parser caps tool detail at `DETAIL_CAP` while parsing, so masking a parsed turn would miss a value crossing that cap. The transcript reader gains an additive `read_masked(handle, &dyn Fn(&str) -> String)` that applies the mask to every string field before `cap`; the port's conversation cache (§4.4) is populated through it, keyed by the secret set's fingerprint as well, and is separate from the UI's unmasked cache. The 256 KiB turn cut then runs on masked text.
198	  - **run output**: `scrollback::tail_text` cuts bytes before stripping escapes and choosing lines. It gains an overlap: the read starts `longest secret length` bytes before the tail window, the mask runs over the whole buffer, and the line selection then discards the overlap; a value straddling the window's first byte is therefore masked whole. A secret value containing a newline is masked only within a line, which the dialog's sentence on redaction covers.
199	  - **screen**: the existing slack-lines read, unchanged.
200	  - **file content**: the file is read whole under its limit, masked, then sent.
201	  - **last response** and the card excerpt: masked from the turn's full text, then cut.
202	  The secret set for a session is the project's secret variables plus its granted sets; for a file it is the owning project's. The set is resolved **before any cached content is returned**, on every read, and its **policy fingerprint** (a hash over the sorted names and values, held in memory only, never logged or stored) is part of every masked cache's version (§4.4): a new grant, a changed value or a removed set makes previously masked bytes stale even when their source did not move. If the secret set cannot be resolved (a Keychain error, a missing set), the reply is **refused** with that reason, never sent unredacted and never served from a cached success. What this covers is exactly the values Switchboard holds: a secret the user pasted into a prompt, or one a tool printed that Switchboard never knew, is not found. The paired-devices dialog says this in a sentence, and the claim in design.md's trust boundary is widened to "or as redacted text on the remote port".
203	
204	New read models, added to the wire crate:
205	
206	- `session.conversation`: the `Conversation` from `ports::transcript` as a wire shape: title, model, branch, usage, and turns paged by **turn number** (`n`, 1-based). The host parses the whole JSONL, as the session view does, from the app-level cache (§4.4); a transcript the app can show is one the port can serve, and the supported size is whatever the app handles, which the spike measures. What paging bounds is the **response**: a page anchored at its start (`from=turn`) stops at `limit` turns or at the body cap, whichever first, and says `next` for the turn to continue from; a page anchored at its end (`from=last`, or `before=turn` for the page ending before a turn the client holds) fills backward from the anchor, so it always reaches it and `from` is wherever it filled up. The client opens on the tail and walks back with `before`, so a transcript whose turns are large never shows a stale end or a gap; a change is followed from the last turn held page after page until `next` is empty, up to ten pages. A page carries only the first 512 bytes of each tool call's input and result and of each activity's text, marked `more`, which is what keeps a turn with a hundred tool calls to tens of kilobytes rather than hundreds; `session.turn` reads one turn whole, at the conversation's revision, and the client asks for it when a turn's activity is opened. A single turn larger than 256 KiB is cut (final text kept whole where possible, activity text trimmed) and marked `truncated`. The page carries the `resume_id` it was read from: `/clear` and a discard rebind the record to a new transcript, and a client holding turn numbers from another handle drops them and refetches from 1. The last turn is always in progress until a `Stop` event: on a `changed {conversation}` the client refetches from the last turn it holds and **replaces** that turn and everything after it. A handle rebind (`resume_id` moved on the session view) changes the conversation cache's key, which emits `changed {conversation}` of its own, so the client needs no rule linking the two. Only Claude Code sessions have a conversation; Codex, shell, command and service sessions answer with a "no conversation" reason and the client falls back to `screen` (and, for commands and services, `run_output`).
207	- `session.last_response`: the last turn's `final_text`, its `n` and `end`. It is a **projection of the `conversation` key**: it is read from the same cache, carries the conversation's content revision, is watched by watching `conversation`, and refreshes on `changed {conversation}`; a window showing only the last response registers that watch. The compact card's one-line excerpt is not part of it: that is `last_message` from the `Stop` hook on the record, a field of the session's metadata, and moves with `changed {session}`.
208	- `session.runs`: a command's or service's runs as the record holds them (`Run`: `n`, started, ended, exit, artifacts' names, not their paths). `session.run_output`: the tail of one run's scrollback log (`scrollback::tail_text`, escapes stripped, `lines` clamped to 500), redacted; a run whose log was pruned or rotated answers with that reason. This is how an exited command whose pane is gone is still readable: `session.screen` refuses a session that is not running, by design.
209	- `file.read`: content of a file **only if some working set pins it** (`PinTarget::File` with that project and path). The read goes through a new `ports::files` method, `read_pinned(root, relative)`, not through the UI's preview loader. Confinement is by descriptors, not by path strings, so it stays valid while names change under it:
210	  - the relative path is rejected if it is absolute, empty, or has a `..` or `.` component, before anything touches the disk (a persisted pin can hold anything);
211	  - the project root is opened once as a directory descriptor (`O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_CLOEXEC`) and the walk proceeds **one component at a time** with `openat` from the previous descriptor: every directory component with `O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK | O_CLOEXEC`, the last with `O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK | O_CLOEXEC`. ### 4.1 Implementation

- **No Tokio.** The host is std threads and `mpsc`; the core is owned by `SwitchboardApp` and every state change is a dispatch on the frame thread. The remote port follows the `ControlSocket` shape: an accept thread per listener, one thread per connection, each request handed over a channel to the frame, answered by the same `serve` path in `app.rs` (`serve_pending` runs before every frame, hidden ones included), the reply sent back on the connection's channel. A second runtime inside an egui app buys nothing for a handful of connections.
- **The frame does core state only.** A metadata request (a view, a command) is answered on the frame as the control port is. A content request (conversation, screen, run output, file) takes two steps: the frame answers with the **handle and the redaction policy** (the transcript path and resume handle, the pane's host id, the run's log path, the file's root and relative path, plus the secret values to mask and the policy fingerprint), and one **content worker thread** does the read, the parse, the mask, the version check and the serialization from a queue of such requests (one at a time, so one large parse is in memory at once; Spike 22 measured 575 MB peak for the largest transcript), then sends one small action back to the frame to record the version it observed (§4.4), and the connection thread writes the reply. The watch poll (§4.4) runs through the same worker. A multi-megabyte transcript, a 768 KiB file or a slow Keychain call therefore costs the worker its time and the asking connection its wait, never a frame. The handle is read under the frame's authority, so a record removed or rebound between the two steps makes the worker's version action a no-op and the reply carries the handle it read from.
- **Bounds.** The port is one user's few devices, and the limits say so:
  - at most 16 connections in total and 4 unauthenticated ones; a further accept is closed at once. The 4 are a separate pool: an unauthenticated flood fills its own slots and never a paired client's;
  - `/pair` is answered at most six times a minute per listener and `/info` sixty; past that the connection thread answers 429 without reaching the frame;
  - a TLS handshake and the first request line each within 5 s, a request body within 10 s, a write within 10 s; a connection that misses a deadline is closed;
  - one request in flight per connection (HTTP/1.1, no pipelining);
  - the frame drains at most 8 remote requests per pass, in arrival order, the rest waiting on the channel; the channel is bounded at 64 and a full channel answers 503 from the connection thread without reaching the frame; a frame-side request is a view or a handle lookup and takes microseconds, so the count is the bound;
  - each WebSocket subscriber has an event queue of 256; when it fills, the subscriber is sent `resync_required` and closed, never silently trimmed (§4.4);
  - the watch set (§4.4) is capped at 128 keys for the whole port; past the cap the least recently read key is evicted silently, since a read of an evicted key always works and re-enters it.
- Preferred crates: a blocking HTTP/1.1 server over `std::net::TcpListener` (hand-rolled or `tiny_http`), `tungstenite` for WebSocket, `rustls` with `rcgen` for the per-installation certificate, and `mdns-sd` (or the system `dns-sd` through a small macOS adapter) for Bonjour. All of it in `src/adapters/remote.rs` behind a `ports::remote` trait with a fake, and all of it must compile on Linux CI (Bonjour may be a `cfg(target_os = "macos")` adapter with a no-op elsewhere). **Spike 22 (§10) decides the exact crates before any of this is built.**
- Handlers are thin: HTTP request → auth and scope check → allowlist → `wire::Request` → `serve` → redaction → `wire::Reply` → HTTP response. No session or transcript logic lives in the adapter.
- Only the instance holding the store lock listens (as the control port does); a read-only instance refuses to bind.
- Bind to loopback by default until remote access is explicitly enabled in Settings. For LAN access, bind the chosen interface and require pairing.
- Configurable port in `identity.json` (§3.1), default `43187`, overridable with `SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT` (a dev aid, documented in the README) so two instances can run on one machine; `0` picks a free one, which the tests use.
- Advertise `_switchboard._tcp` via Bonjour only while listening on a non-loopback interface. TXT records carry the protocol major version (`v`), the display name (`name`) and the `server_id` (`id`, so a client matches a record to a known server before it connects); never a token, never key material. The instance name is the display name with a short id suffix, so two installations on one machine stay distinct.
- If Switchboard closes, the port goes away. A standalone daemon is not in scope.

### 4.2 API conventions

- Version prefix: `/api/v1`.
- JSON request and response bodies. Timestamps as milliseconds since the epoch, matching the wire crate (`last_stop_at_ms`); the client formats them.
- The wire crate's views are the response schemas. New views are added to `switchboard-control` additively (it stays std + serde only, and Dispatch keeps compiling).
- Standard error shape: `{ "error": { "code": "...", "message": "..." } }`, with `wire::Reply::Failed` mapped onto it.
- **Every response** carries the host's `epoch` and `revision` (§4.4) in an envelope: `{ "epoch": "...", "revision": n, "body": ... }`. The revision is the one at which the body's **content version** was observed (§4.4, "Content versions"), not merely the counter at the time of the reply. The client keeps one held revision per resource key (a session's metadata, its conversation, its screen, one run's output, one file are separate keys) and applies a reply only if its revision is at or past the held one, so an older reply arriving after a newer one is dropped and fetching a session's metadata never invalidates a valid conversation page.
- **Caps.** The serialized, masked body of any reply is at most 1 MiB, envelope included, enforced on the output bytes. The rule per kind:
  - **collections** (`projects`, `spaces`, `sets`, `sessions`, `runs`, a set's pins, `waiting`) are answered **whole, in one reply, never paged and never cut**. They are small: a data directory holds hundreds of records at most, and a project's session list with every string bounded as below is under 100 KiB at that scale. A collection reply is one snapshot of its membership at one revision, which is what makes a cached member's removal safe: a member missing from a whole reply at a revision at or past the one it was learned at is gone. The 1 MiB cap is enforced on the serialized reply as everywhere; a collection that would exceed it is a bug in the bounds, answered `too_large` and logged, not paged around.
  - **metadata views**, in a collection and standing alone, are bounded field by field, after masking: `notes` at 4 KiB in a collection and 64 KiB standing alone, `name`, `waiting_reason`, `cwd` and every other free-text string at 4 KiB, each cut marked in a `truncated` list of field names; no field is left unbounded. A client that wants a session's full notes reads the session alone.
  - **conversation** pages stop at `limit` turns or at the cap with `next`; a turn larger than 256 KiB is cut and marked (§4.3).
  - **last response** and **run output** are cut from the front (older text dropped) and marked `truncated: true`.
  - **file content** is sent whole or not at all: the port's file limit is 768 KiB of source bytes, and a larger pinned file answers `too_large` with its size. The source limit is not a guarantee of fit: JSON escaping can double a file of quotation marks and masking can lengthen text, so the limit is enforced once more on the masked, serialized reply, and a file that exceeds it there answers `too_large` too, naming the serialized size. The client says so on the card.
  - **screen** is bounded by `lines` (at most 200) and, after masking, by bytes: text over 256 KiB is cut from the top (older lines dropped) and marked `truncated: true`.
- A command is **accepted** when `serve` returns; its outcome arrives through events and the session's state. For `session.send` there is no completion signal beyond the next `Stop` hook event on that record (§4.5).
- Document payload schemas with examples; generate the Swift `Codable` types from the Rust views (serde shapes) and keep a fixture test on both sides.

  - **run output**: `scrollback::tail_text` cuts bytes before stripping escapes and choosing lines. It gains an overlap: the read starts `longest secret length` bytes before the tail window, the mask runs over the whole buffer, and the line selection then discards the overlap; a value straddling the window's first byte is therefore masked whole. A secret value containing a newline is masked only within a line, which the dialog's sentence on redaction covers.

  - **file content**: the file is read whole under its limit, masked, then sent.

I wrote four objections to `plan.feedback-1.md`. All four rest on the tree; none needed web evidence.

1. **The card excerpt.** The spec already defines the excerpt as the session's `last_message`, masked, and refreshed when the session changes (`docs/remote-client.md:201,207`). The plan replaces it with one `last-response` fetch per Claude session, which the issue didn't ask for. It justifies this by saying the list never touches the 128-key watch set, but that's false: every content read adds its key to that set for a minute (`src/app.rs:2111`, `:1754-1768`). So a polling page can push out a headset's keys, and each first fetch parses a whole transcript on the single content worker. The plan's worry about masking is fair, since the tree resolves the masking policy on the worker, but the answer is to mask `last_message` as the spec says.
2. **The planned test that no `/api/v1/…` path in `app.js` answers `404 not_found` can't pass as written.** With a random UUID filled in, content reads answer exactly `404 not_found` ("no such session") at `src/app.rs:1856-1861`. The test needs seeded ids, or a way to tell that refusal apart from the allowlist's.
3. **Two line references are off by one or two.** `bind_remote` is at `src/app.rs:2936`, not 2935, and `Limits` is at `src/adapters/remote.rs:623-639`, not 625-640. The other references I checked are correct.
4. **The `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION` bump never reaches an existing install.** `update_identity` only changes what it is told to (`src/core/remote.rs:105-117`), and only `make_identity` sets the version. An upgraded `identity.json` would get the two new fields but still say version 1, so the `CertificateReissued` handler has to set it.

I did not object to the HttpOnly cookie, though how it behaves in browsers is still open. Your rules protect the cookie as the safer place for the token, and my two searches (whether a `Secure` cookie survives a certificate click-through, and whether `__Host-` works on an IP host) found nothing primary either way. The other decisions I checked against the tree held up, including the Origin rule, `include_str!` paths, `__Host-` attributes, the 400-day `Max-Age`, the pool and `Connection: close`, and the reissue over the same key.

I couldn't read issue #230 itself (`gh` needed approval), so I took the plan's quotes of the issue as given when judging what the issue asks to change.
